unitTargets: S03.1  I can identify a mineral using its physical properties.
S03.5  I can trace how any rock becomes any other rock.
S03.2  I can classify igneous rocks by texture and composition.
S03.3  I can classify sedimentary rocks by grain size and origin.
S03.4  I can identify a metamorphic rock and its parent rock.
howItWorks: These notes follow the slides in order. Each block is one slide.
The SLIDE number on the left matches the number in the top corner of the slide on the board.
Write what the slide shows in the blanks, tables and flowcharts.
A gray rule down the left of a line means must-write. Copy it exactly.
Each section ends with a RECALL block. Close your notes before you write it.

sectionsContent.title: Minerals & Mineral ID
sectionsContent.learningTarget: I can identify a mineral using its physical properties.

rows.title: Slide 03
cues: Record: the five characteristics
lead: *A mineral must meet all five characteristics.

rows.title: Slide 04
cues: Record: each formula and its key clue
lead: *Use several properties together. Color alone is not enough.

rows.title: Slide 05
cues: Record: streak and the two kinds of luster

notes.text: The outside color can change. Test the powder too.

notes.prompt: Hematite may look ______________. Its streak is ______________.
notes.answer: Hematite may look silver-black. Its streak is red-brown.

notes: *Describe the shine before you guess the mineral.

rows.title: Slide 06
cues: Record: the definition and the field tools

rows.title: Slide 07
cues: Record: how each sample breaks or reacts

lead.answer: Cleavage breaks along flat planes. Fracture breaks unevenly.

rows.title: Slide 08
cues: Record: the observations and test results

lead.text: Choose the best match. Use the test results as evidence.

rows.title: Slide 09
cues: Record: the ID and the clues that support it

notes.answer: Strong clues: hardness about 6; two cleavage planes near 90°
Supporting clues: pink color, white streak, and glassy luster

notes: *Color helps, but hardness and cleavage narrow the choices.

rows.title: Slide 10
cues: Record: the lab routine

notes.text: At each station: observe color and luster, test streak and hardness, and look for cleavage or fracture. Record your observations on the lab handout.

rows.title: Section summary
cues: Close your notes before you write.
rows.prompt: Explain how to identify a mineral. Use at least three properties.
rows.answer: Observe color and luster, then test streak and hardness and look for cleavage or fracture. Color alone is not enough; streak, hardness and cleavage narrow it down.
selfCheck: I can list the five characteristics of a mineral.
I can explain why streak is more useful than color.
I can use hardness and cleavage to identify a mineral.

sectionsContent.title: The Rock Cycle
sectionsContent.learningTarget: I can trace how any rock becomes any other rock.

rows.title: Slide 11
cues: Record: how each rock family forms

rows: Sediment builds up, or minerals form from water.
Heat and pressure change an existing rock.

rows.title: Slide 12
cues: Record: the definition and the sandstone steps

lead.prompt: A rock is a natural solid, usually made of one or more ______________.
lead.answer: A rock is a natural solid, usually made of one or more minerals.

lead.prompt: Minerals are the ______________. Some rocks also contain glass or organic material.
lead.answer: Minerals are the ingredients. Some rocks also contain glass or organic material.

lead.label: One way to make a rock: sediment becomes sandstone

rows.title: Slide 13
cues: Record: the three rock types
Record: the process on each arrow
notes: *No single starting point. Any exposed rock can become sediment.

rows.title: Slide 14
cues: Record: the rock at each step

lead.text: Quartz grains can survive weathering and become part of a new rock.

rows.title: Slide 15
cues: Record: the starting and ending rock

notes.text: Name the process. Decide whether the rock needs to melt. The next slide gives the route.

rows.title: Slide 16
cues: Record: the route

lead.prompt: Heat and pressure can change basalt while it stays ______________.
lead.answer: Heat and pressure can change basalt while it stays solid.

rows.title: Section summary
cues: Close your notes before you write.
rows.prompt: Describe one path a rock can take through the rock cycle. Name each process.
rows.answer: Granite weathers and erodes into sediment; the sand deposits and cements into sandstone; heat and pressure change it to quartzite without melting.
selfCheck: I can name the three rock families and how each forms.
I can label the rock cycle.
I can explain why metamorphism does not need melting.

sectionsContent.title: Igneous Rocks
sectionsContent.learningTarget: I can classify igneous rocks by texture and composition.

rows.title: Slide 18
cues: Record: where each cools and its crystal size
notes: *Both form when melted rock cools and hardens.

rows.title: Slide 19
cues: Record: what each kind of cooling makes

lead.text: Texture describes crystal size and other visible features.

rows: Crystals may not have time to form

rows.title: Slide 20
cues: Record: the rock each cooling rate makes

notes.text: Same general composition. Different time to grow crystals.

rows.title: Slide 21
cues: Record: what each texture looks like

lead.text: Texture describes the size and arrangement of crystals.

rows: Crystals too small to see easily
Large crystals in a finer background

rows.title: Slide 22
cues: Record: the example, color and silica for each group
lead: *The minerals in a rock affect its color.

rows: Least silica; rich in Fe + Mg

rows.title: Slide 23
cues: Record: each mineral, in the order it forms
lead: *As magma cools, different minerals can form.

rows.title: Slide 24
cues: Record: the rock for each texture and composition

lead.text: Match crystal size with composition. Use the other textures too.

rows.title: Slide 25
cues: Record: the texture and composition clues

lead.text: Describe the texture first. Then decide the composition.

rows: Coarse grains. Crystals are easy to see.
Mostly light-colored. Pink, clear, and black grains.

rows.title: Slide 26
cues: Record: the ID and what each clue means
lead: *Large crystals tell us the rock cooled slowly underground.

rows: Usually rich in quartz and feldspar

rows.title: Slide 27
cues: Record: the lab routine

notes.text: At each station: describe the texture, estimate the composition, and use the ID chart to name the rock. Record your observations on the lab handout.

rows.title: Section summary
cues: Close your notes before you write.
rows.prompt: Explain how texture and composition together identify an igneous rock.
rows.answer: Crystal size shows how fast it cooled (coarse = slow, inside Earth; fine = fast, at the surface). Color shows composition (light = felsic, dark = mafic). The chart matches the two.
selfCheck: I can tell intrusive from extrusive rocks by crystal size.
I can name the felsic, intermediate and mafic rocks.
I can put Bowen's minerals in order.

sectionsContent.title: Sedimentary Rocks
sectionsContent.learningTarget: I can classify sedimentary rocks by grain size and origin.

rows.title: Slide 29
cues: Record: the four steps and the two parts of lithification

lead.text: For clastic rocks, loose pieces become solid rock.

notes.answer: Compaction: burial squeezes the grains together.
Cementation: minerals glue the grains together.

rows.title: Slide 30
cues: Record: what happens at each stage

lead.text: Burial packs the grains. Mineral cement helps hold them together.

rows.title: Slide 31
cues: Record: how each type forms, with an example
lead: *The type depends on where the material came from.

rows.title: Slide 32
cues: Record: the size and the rock for each grain

lead.text: Look at the pieces that make up the rock.

rows.title: Slide 33
cues: Record: the clue for each rock

lead.text: Look at the grains, their shapes, and how they fit together.

rows.title: Slide 34
cues: Record: the rock at the end of each path

lead.text: Start with visible grains. Confirm the ID with another clue.

notes.answer: Other clues: layers, fossils, ripple marks, and mud cracks.

rows.title: Slide 35
cues: Record: what you see and how it holds together

lead.text: Use grain size and shape to support your answer.

rows: Rounded pebbles. Smaller sand grains between them.
The pieces are cemented into rock.

rows.title: Slide 36
cues: Record: the ID and the key clues
lead: *Rounded gravel-sized pieces are the key clue.

rows: Rounded pieces help separate it from breccia.

rows.title: Slide 37
cues: Record: the lab routine

notes.text: At each station: look for grain size and shape, check for layers or fossils, and use only the approved acid test. Record your observations on the lab handout.

rows.title: Section summary
cues: Close your notes before you write.
rows.prompt: Explain how grain size and grain shape help identify a sedimentary rock.
rows.answer: Grain size sorts clay (shale), sand (sandstone) and gravel; for gravel, rounded pieces mean conglomerate and angular pieces mean breccia. No visible grains: check for fizzing (limestone) or plant material (coal).
selfCheck: I can put the steps of sedimentary rock formation in order.
I can name the three types of sedimentary rock.
I can tell conglomerate from breccia.

sectionsContent.title: Metamorphic Rocks
sectionsContent.learningTarget: I can identify a metamorphic rock and its parent rock.

rows.title: Slide 39
cues: Record: the two kinds of metamorphism

lead.prompt: Metamorphism changes an existing rock without ______________ it.
lead.answer: Metamorphism changes an existing rock without melting it.

notes: *The rock stays solid. If it melts and then cools, the new rock is igneous.

rows.title: Slide 40
cues: Record: what pressure does to flat minerals

lead.prompt: Pressure can help ______________ minerals line up as the rock changes.
lead.answer: Pressure can help flat minerals line up as the rock changes.

notes.answer: Before: minerals point in different directions.
After directed pressure: flat minerals align. The rock stays solid.

rows.title: Slide 41
cues: Record: what each looks like
lead: *Foliation is a pattern of aligned minerals or mineral bands.

rows: Minerals line up or form bands.
No clear layers or mineral alignment.

rows.title: Slide 42
cues: Record: each rock in the sequence

lead.answer: Grade describes the intensity of metamorphism.

rows.title: Slide 43
cues: Record: what each parent becomes

lead.answer: The parent rock is the rock you started with.

rows.title: Slide 44
cues: Record: the rock at the end of each path

lead.text: Use texture first. Then test the mineral clues.

rows.title: Slide 45
cues: Record: the pattern and texture

lead.text: Describe the pattern before naming the rock.

rows: Coarse grains. Minerals are easy to see.

rows.title: Slide 46
cues: Record: the ID, family and parent rocks
lead: *The mineral bands are the strongest clue.

rows: Granite or shale. The original composition matters.

rows.title: Slide 47
cues: Record: the lab routine

notes.text: At each station: look for foliation, describe grains, sheen or bands, and match each rock to a possible parent. Record your observations on the lab handout.

rows.title: Section summary
cues: Close your notes before you write.
rows.prompt: Explain how to identify a metamorphic rock and name a possible parent rock.
rows.answer: Look for foliation first: slate, phyllite, schist and gneiss are foliated. Non-foliated: marble fizzes, quartzite scratches glass. Marble comes from limestone; quartzite from sandstone.
selfCheck: I can tell contact from regional metamorphism.
I can put slate, phyllite, schist and gneiss in order of grade.
I can match a metamorphic rock to its parent rock.
